claims.claim: Century Aluminum occupies a primary-material bottleneck linking electricity and alumina inputs to domestic aluminum supply used across transport, construction, grid and defense infrastructure; Mt. Holly expansion increases existing U.S. output while the planned Oklahoma smelter would materially expand domestic capacity if financed, built and powered as planned.

The successor bottleneck is energy-intensive production economics: new domestic capacity only improves resilience durably if power supply, alumina, construction cost, operating reliability and commodity spreads support competitive production.

causalEdges: electricity + alumina -> smelting capacity -> primary aluminum -> industrial/infrastructure supply resilience
new domestic smelter -> reduced import dependence -> resilience, conditional on competitive operating economics
power reliability/cost -> smelter utilization/margin -> durable domestic capacity

risks.risk: Domestic capacity can strengthen supply resilience while shifting the critical constraint to large, reliable and competitively priced power supply.

unknowns.unknown: Final Oklahoma capital structure, schedule, power arrangement and Century funding burden are not established in cited evidence.

claims.claim: Q2 liquidity and EBITDA support current execution capacity, but exceptional Iceland equipment failures demonstrate that smelter reliability can materially affect results; current profitability should not be extrapolated without normalizing aluminum premiums, power and operational disruptions.
The Oklahoma project is structurally meaningful but remains financing/execution optionality until capital burden, schedule and power economics are sufficiently evidenced.

causalEdges: commodity premium + power cost + reliability -> EBITDA/cash flow -> funding capacity -> expansion execution

risks.risk: Commodity-price and regional premium exposure can reverse favorable earnings quickly.
Power cost/availability is both a strategic enabler and a concentration risk for smelting economics.
Large-project financing and construction can create dilution, leverage or schedule risk depending on final structure.

unknowns.unknown: Normalized profitability and final Oklahoma financing/dilution exposure remain unquantified.
